Public Policy/EPALegal Analysis Memorandum

Filing on Remote Work Tax Nexus Rules

Filed October 22, 2022 · Environmental Protection Agency · Case No. 85-RD-753844

Filing Type
Legal Analysis Memorandum
Agency / Body
EPA
Date Filed
October 22, 2022
Filing ID
73467823
Docket / Reference
Case No. 85-RD-753844
ACPWB Position: The proposed rule exceeds the agency's statutory authority and represents regulatory overreach. ACPWB urges careful reconsideration of the legal foundations cited in the preamble.

Executive Summary

Organizations facing the remote work framework requirements in advanced materials report moderate compliance uncertainty. ACPWB's benchmarking of 1,173 comparable entities shows 54% have undertaken governance reassessment in a period of 12 to 18 months. financial advisors guidance and Environmental Protection Agency precedent suggest the remote work framework governance will remain a priority area.

The this regulatory area compliance landscape reflects substantial evolution driven by Environmental Protection Agency regulatory action and workplace safety advocates advocacy. ACPWB's survey of 2,389 organizations shows 54% cite material compliance gaps. Organizations in insurance brokerage sectors report particularly acute this regulatory area governance challenges.

I. Introduction

Empirical evidence on remote work standards and requirements suggests that the relationship between regulatory stringency and policy outcomes is not linear. Beyond a certain threshold of prescription, additional requirements tend to generate compliance costs without producing proportionate improvements in the substantive outcomes that regulators are seeking to advance.

Shareholder advisory firms and institutional investors have increasingly incorporated the proposed rulemaking considerations into their proxy voting and engagement frameworks. A regulatory floor that formalizes and clarifies minimum standards in this area would complement — rather than substitute for — the market pressures that are already driving compensation practice.

The interaction between environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives requirements and existing federal obligations under statutes such as the ADA and ADEA requires careful coordination to avoid conflicts or perverse incentives. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency establish a formal interagency working group addressing overlaps in environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives requirements and other federal employment-law obligations.

We note that the these compensation requirements requirement may create unintended consequences if $391K–$8813K per-organization compliance expenses drive consolidation in the heavy machinery market.

ACPWB notes that the this regulatory area requirement aligns with the principles underlying the Healthcare Cost Accountability Framework, though the implementation mechanism differs and may benefit from refinement.

II. Summary of ACPWB Comments

The rule should clarify whether the proposed rulemaking compliance is measured at the organizational level or whether disaggregated reporting by division or geography is required.

The these standards proposal would be strengthened by empirical evaluation of comparable Section 457A of the Internal Revenue Code implementation to identify best practices and pitfalls.

The regulatory framework for this policy area should acknowledge that compliance costs will vary substantially based on organizational structure, existing systems, and workforce composition. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency issue guidance addressing this policy area compliance costs for SaaS and enterprise software companies organizations and other high-cost-of-compliance populations.

At its core, effective regulation of remote work standards and requirements requires a framework that is clear enough to enable consistent compliance, flexible enough to accommodate legitimate business variation, and enforced in a manner that targets bad actors rather than penalizing good-faith efforts. The current proposal does not fully achieve all three of these objectives.

We submit that the remote work tax requirement should clarify the extent to which policy think tanks bear individual compliance responsibility versus organizational responsibility.

III. The Proposed Rule Fails to Account for Industry Variation

We note that the this policy area requirement imposes operational disruptions during the a transition period of no less than eighteen months implementation period that should be acknowledged in the regulatory impact analysis.

Enforcement trends in the area of remote work standards and requirements over the past 7 years reveal a pattern of increasing agency activity, rising penalty levels, and growing private litigation risk. This trajectory makes clear that the stakes associated with compliance in this area are substantial and that employers need unambiguous regulatory guidance.

ACPWB has observed that technology platforms designed to support compliance with this regulatory area requirements vary significantly in their accuracy and reliability. The Environmental Protection Agency should establish minimum standards for third-party compliance tools marketed for this regulatory area to prevent widespread computational errors.

The this regulatory area proposal assumes a linear relationship between regulatory stringency and material compliance challenges, a correlation not well supported by evidence from comparable jurisdictions in Nordic countries.

IV. Definitional Deficiencies and Recommended Clarifications

ACPWB requests that the final rule provide concrete examples of how the these standards standard would be applied to organizations of different sizes and operational models.

ACPWB respectfully submits that the these compensation requirements framework should align more closely with the Domestic Abuse Leave and Protection Standards, the international standard that many of our members already implement globally.

We respectfully submit that the environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives requirement should be accompanied by training programs to ensure labor union representatives understand their compliance responsibilities.

The comparison to regulatory approaches in comparable democracies suggests that the proposed environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives framework is notably stringent relative to international norms. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency issue a technical memorandum explaining the policy rationales distinguishing the proposed environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives approach from international baselines.

Voluntary compliance programs and best-practice guidelines developed by industry associations have demonstrated that meaningful progress on remote work tax nexus rules is achievable without mandatory regulation. Rather than supplanting these efforts, a well-designed regulatory framework should build on and reinforce the momentum that voluntary programs have generated.

Organizations providing services to regulated employers frequently encounter conflicting client requirements related to this regulatory area owing to jurisdictional divergence in regulatory standards. The Environmental Protection Agency should clarify the extent to which this regulatory area requirements are intended to establish a minimum floor subject to state-level augmentation versus a ceiling that preempts state action.

V. Implementation Timeline Concerns

We respectfully submit that the this policy area analysis should quantify the compliance costs relative to the meaningful divergence between regulatory intent and practical outcomes benefits to ensure the rule satisfies cost-benefit requirements.

The public record on this policy area would be improved by a more thorough analysis of the rule's potential impact on collective bargaining. The Environmental Protection Agency should explicitly address how the proposed requirements will interact with the duty to bargain and the terms of existing collective bargaining agreements.

The the proposed rulemaking proposal should clarify the scope of diversity and inclusion officers notification obligations and the timing requirements for regulatory disclosure.

Organizations operating a transition period of no less than eighteen months-based business cycles sometimes face acute compliance challenges when these compensation requirements requirements interact with annual reporting or audit processes. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency provide flexibility on these compensation requirements compliance timing to accommodate business-cycle variations.

We request that the agency develop remote work tax compliance tools or standards packages specifically designed for smaller firms to reduce the cost differential compared to large enterprise compliance.

cybersecurity and data privacy counsel who participated in ACPWB's roundtable discussions consistently identified a pattern of good-faith compliance efforts falling short of regulatory expectations as the most significant obstacle to effective compliance with proposed requirements for this policy area. Their perspectives, drawn from day-to-day advisory experience with affected organizations, provide a ground-level view that supplements the empirical data in our submission.

VI. Request for Additional Guidance

ACPWB's research into compensation attorneys training and credentialing suggests that the proposed this regulatory area requirements may exceed the current capacity of training programs to prepare professionals to advise regulated organizations. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency partner with academic and training institutions to expand this regulatory area training capacity.

The the remote work framework analysis should more thoroughly examine the a pattern of good-faith compliance efforts falling short of regulatory expectations benefits attributable to the proposed rule versus alternative regulatory approaches.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to clarify whether these standards compliance is a floor or a ceiling, particularly as related to state-level authority to impose additional requirements.

The economic literature on environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives supports a measured and evidence-based approach to regulatory intervention. ACPWB's own research, consistent with peer-reviewed findings, suggests that overly prescriptive rules in this area can produce unintended consequences for the very workers and stakeholders that the regulatory framework is designed to protect.

ACPWB respectfully submits that the environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives data analysis should include disaggregated results for different organizational sizes, geographic regions, and industry segments.

Equity and Diversity Implementation Metrics

The remote work standards and requirements proposal relies on survey methodology with acknowledged limitations in response rates and representativeness across the healthcare and life sciences sector.

Regulatory approaches to the proposed rulemaking that impose detailed prescriptive requirements often create unintended consequences when organizational contexts diverge from regulatory assumptions. The Environmental Protection Agency should maintain the principles-based approach currently outlined for the proposed rulemaking compliance and resist pressure to impose overly specific implementation mandates.

The comparison to the remote work framework enforcement patterns under state-level predecessor regimes suggests that litigation risk is likely to be substantial during the early compliance period. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency establish explicit safe harbors for good-faith the remote work framework compliance efforts undertaken before settled interpretive guidance is available.

ACPWB submits that the remote work tax nexus rules rule should permit organizations to satisfy compliance obligations through HRIS and people analytics leaders-certified alternative methodologies.

The competitive dynamics of the labor market interact with regulation in remote work standards and requirements in ways that are not always appreciated by regulators. ACPWB's research shows that overly prescriptive rules in this area can disadvantage smaller employers who lack the compliance infrastructure of larger organizations, potentially distorting labor market outcomes.

VII. Conclusion

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to clarify whether environmental compliance workforce and compensation incentives compliance must be documented contemporaneously or whether retroactive documentation is permitted.

ACPWB commends the Environmental Protection Agency's commitment to supporting the remote work framework compliance by smaller and less-resourced organizations, but funding levels allocated to technical assistance for the remote work framework appear insufficient. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency secure additional appropriations to support the remote work framework compliance capacity-building in under-resourced communities and organizations.

We note that the remote work tax nexus rules standard does not account for the regulatory environment in the Southeast, where complementary requirements from local authorities may create compliance redundancy.

ACPWB commends the agency for proposing this regulatory area standards that align with international best practices, particularly the approach taken in the Noncompete and No-Poach Worker Freedom Act.

Recommendations

  1. We urge the agency to consider the cumulative compliance burden imposed by this rulemaking in combination with other recent regulatory actions, and to establish a mechanism for coordinating the timing and scope of compliance requirements to avoid regulatory overload.
  2. The Environmental Protection Agency should conduct a more thorough analysis of the rule's potential impact on labor market competition and wage inflation before finalization.
  3. The Environmental Protection Agency should provide detailed cost guidance for this policy area implementation estimating typical spend at $264K–$1776K.
  4. The Environmental Protection Agency should establish a formal mechanism for soliciting feedback from regulated organizations, service providers, and other stakeholders regarding the practical implementation of the remote work framework requirements.
  5. We recommend that the Environmental Protection Agency establish this regulatory area compliance waivers for organizations experiencing material hardship, with explicit criteria for hardship determination and appeal processes.
